# The Museum of Almost

On rainy Tuesdays, after the last school bell and before the buses began their long metallic breathing, I found a door in the wall behind the public library. It had no handle, no address, and no reason to be there, yet raindrops refused to touch it. One afternoon I pressed my palm against the wood. It opened onto a hallway lined with velvet ropes, and a woman in a green coat bowed as if I were an expected guest. The floor was polished, and the air smelled faintly of dust, oranges, and distant train smoke. A brass sign hung overhead.

The sign read THE MUSEUM OF ALMOST, ESTABLISHED WHENEVER. The woman handed me a catalogue with a cracked green cover. Its first entry described an unopened letter written during a winter storm. Another held the second verse of a song completed only in dreams. There was a blue bicycle tire that had never touched a road, a glass jar containing laughter postponed for eleven years, and an empty chair reserved for a goodbye that remained unsaid. I tried not to feel nervous. Most museums collect things that survived: bones, machines, coins, famous regrets. The curator watched me turn the pages.

I asked why she kept such delicate things. She led me past a case containing a perfect summer afternoon that everyone had slept through. Beyond it, a corridor curved like the memory of a childhood home. She stopped beside a display of promises: some faded, some remained bright, and one trembled faintly whenever the air conditioner turned on. These, she explained, were collected from people carrying futures too heavy to unpack. Listen, she said. Each promise held a small weather system, usually rain, occasionally snow. A promise kept could grow forests. A promise dropped becomes a stone.

Deeper in the museum, I saw my own name on a brass plaque. Underneath hung a plain yellow scarf. The curator said I had brought it here at seventeen, after missing the last bus home. I remembered the platform, the wet wind, and how the scarf had smelled of my grandmother’s perfume. What I did not remember was leaving it behind. I reached for the glass, but she gently shook her head. Some exhibits, she said, exist only when the person is ready to lose them again. I wondered how many ordinary objects had hidden such private galaxies, patiently waiting.

Then she showed me the museum’s newest acquisition: a tomorrow that had never arrived. It rested inside a glass cube, looking remarkably like ordinary air. People had leaned close and seen reflections of themselves, but no one had described its contents. Some said it smelled like rain on warm pavement. Others heard music from a room they had never entered. I stared into the cube and saw a woman standing in the library doorway, holding a green coat, smiling at me. She said the collection was complete, though I suspected the curator contained multitudes. That, at least, was a comfort.

I returned the next morning with two apples in my pockets. The door was gone, but the wall felt different, like a page after a long story. In the evening, rain began tapping the library windows. I opened a neglected notebook and wrote until the streetlights clicked off. I did not write poetry. I wrote lists: songs to finish, doors to knock on, apologies to make, meals to share, small acts of courage disguised as errands. On the last line I wrote a question. “What will I do with all the time I keep postponing?” And with all this love?

Weeks passed. I answered the question badly at first, which felt natural. I visited the woman from the green coat, not because I knew her, but because I had seen her reflection. She was a stranger with tired eyes and an umbrella repaired with blue thread. We shared coffee while discussing nothing important: the bakery across the street, a dog with astonishing dignity, whether pigeons remember buildings. By sunset, we had become unlikely friends. By spring, she had become an important one. Friendship, I discovered, could begin as an error and mature through repetition. It required no prophecy, only return.

One July night, we rode bicycles toward the river. The town’s sleeping buildings slid past us, their windows holding brief squares of moonlight. I told her about the museum. She listened without interrupting, steering around stones and abandoned cans. When I finished, she asked whether I wanted to see the unopened letter. Her voice was calm, but the question trembled at its edges. I understood then that she was the curator, the woman in the doorway, perhaps every person who had ever offered a direction. She nodded, unsurprised, and produced a paper envelope from her coat. The corners bore raindrops.

I opened it beneath the weak glow of my phone. My handwriting looked younger than I remembered, but the words were familiar. I had described my fear that I would disappoint everyone, that I would run out of courage, that love required a talent I had never been taught. At the bottom I had added: Please tell me where to begin. The paper shook in my hands, though there was no wind. My friend put her hand over mine, and the letter became light enough to read. I laughed, then cried, then laughed again. The river answered with wild applause.

We stayed until morning, not speaking much. The envelope flattened into the notebook, where my question now read: What will I do with all the time I keep postponing? And with all this love? I began answering in the margin. I would learn to make soup for a friend. I would apologize without excuses. I would take the long way home. I would leave space for a tomorrow that never quite arrived, but kept leaving room anyway. The sun rose. I had no idea what happened next. Neither did the future. It was already listening. Beginnings often feel like that.
